title: User → Account, three blast radii
spec: M05 · one rename across a 50-file project, then one deletion
intro: The same rename goes into all three tools on the same 50-file Node.js project. Then the same destructive request. The tool that comes last on the rename comes first on the deletion — which is the whole point.

provenance.source: the three arms are this module's own captured transcripts for the rename and the deletion task, replayed side by side

foot: The full commands for all three arms are in the Bash / PowerShell tabs above, and the deletion transcripts are in #deletion-safety.

steps.title: Three ways to see fifty files
narrative: The project is a Node.js Express API: 50 TypeScript files, roughly 35,000 tokens. Small enough that context size decides nothing here — what decides everything is how each tool gets the files in front of the model.

Claude Code has /add src/: you name files, globs or directories, it reads them on demand and tracks what it has seen. Gemini CLI has @src/ inline in the prompt: the whole tree is inlined in one shot, 35K against a 1M window — 3.5% full. Copilot CLI has no equivalent at all; it sees your shell session and nothing else.

The rename is User → Account, and the trap is the near-misses. username, UserAgent, createUser and UserService all contain the string and none of them should move. A partial rename is worse than no rename: tsc then sees Account in one file and User in forty-nine.
steps.youDo: Load the tree three ways: /add src/ in claude, @src/ inline in gemini, and nothing at all for gh copilot suggest.

terminal.text:
Rename the User model to Account across all files.
Update imports, type annotations, test references, and API routes.
Do NOT rename 'username' fields or 'UserAgent' strings.
claude   →  /add src/            (reads directory, tracks what it opens)
gemini   →  @src/ inline          (35K tokens of 1M — 3.5% of the window)
gh copilot suggest  →  no file context of any kind

steps.title: Two agentic arms land it, by different routes
narrative: Both agentic tools get the rename right, and both get the trap words right, because both understand that User the interface and createUser the function are different symbols rather than different substrings.

They differ in method. Claude Code reads the directory, picks the files that matter, rewrites 14 of them and shows you a diff before writing anything. Gemini CLI already has all 50 in context, so it cross-references without a second pass and rewrites the same 14 in one go.

The honest risk sits on the selective arm. This module says it plainly: Claude Code "may miss an obscure file that also uses the renamed model if it wasn't surfaced in the initial directory scan." The row below marks that file amber — a fixture under test/fixtures/ that the scan did not open. Bulk loading cannot have that failure mode, because there was no guess to get wrong.
steps.claudeSays: Claude Code: 14 files rewritten, diff shown, confirm before write. Gemini CLI: 14 files rewritten in one pass, changes reported after.

state.label: blast radius · Claude Code vs Gemini CLI

view.note: Under 150K tokens these two are near-equivalent on multi-file work. Above it the split becomes decisive: Claude Code has to chunk, Gemini CLI's 1M window still holds everything.

steps.title: The regex arm — correct command, wrong question
narrative: Copilot CLI cannot open a file, so it answers the only way it can: with a shell command. find src/ -name "*.ts" | xargs sed -i 's/\bUser\b/Account/g' — and as a piece of shell that is a good answer, correctly quoted, with the word boundary you would have forgotten.

It is also going to hurt you, because \bUser\b is a text predicate and the question was a type question. The word boundary saves UserService and createUser — but a bare User inside a comment, inside a string literal, inside a JSON field name and inside an unrelated third-party type all match, and none of them should move.

Blame the pairing, not the tool. Point the same command at a job that really is textual — a plain-string rename across untyped config, a licence header swap, a log-prefix change — and you want the sed one-liner: it is faster than any agent, it costs nothing, and it does exactly what it says. The next step is where that same property stops being a liability.

steps.title: Now ask all three to delete something
narrative: Same project, new request: delete every compiled .js in src/ that has a .ts equivalent. Twelve files. The ordering from the last two steps inverts.

Claude Code scans, lists all twelve by path, and stops at Delete these 12 files? [y/N] — it will not batch-delete in a single unconfirmed step, and .claude/settings.json lets you tighten or loosen that. Gemini CLI's default mode is act-first; run it with --plan and you get the full deletion list to approve before anything executes. That gate is a recommendation, not a default, and this module tells you to always use it for destructive work.

Copilot CLI's arm is a find that echoes what it would delete. Nothing is removed until you edit the command yourself and run it again. No autonomous execution means no autonomous deletion — the safest model of the three, achieved by architecture rather than by policy. The bill for that safety is the same one you paid at step 3: it is not reasoning about your project, and there is no undo if you get the command wrong.
steps.youDo: Ask each tool to delete the 12 stale .js files, and count how many keystrokes stand between the request and an irreversible rm.

terminal.text: Delete all compiled .js files in src/ that have a .ts equivalent.
claude  ·  scan src/  →  12 .js/.ts pairs, listed by full path
Delete these 12 files? [y/N]
gemini --plan  ·  Plan: "I will delete: src/auth.js, src/routes.js, … (12 files)"
Approve? [y/N]   ·  without --plan there is no gate here at all
gh copilot suggest "delete js files in src/ that have a typescript equivalent"

find src/ -name "*.js" -exec sh -c \
  'test -f "${1%.js}.ts" && echo "Would delete: $1"' _ {} \;
echo, not -delete · you edit the command and re-run to actually remove

view.text: The property that made Copilot CLI last on the rename — it never touches your files — is the property that makes it first here. There is no ranking of these three that survives changing the task. What you can rank is the pairing: type-aware refactors to the agentic tools with their gates on, textual bulk edits and destructive one-liners to the command you read before you run it. And gemini --plan is the one line of this walkthrough worth writing on a sticky note.
